plates.title: GIVE THE POINT A BODY
plates.prompt:
Use case: illustration-story. Create a new companion teaching comic using the supplied image as a STYLE AND CHARACTER REFERENCE, not as content to reproduce. Portrait book plate, high resolution, six large panels in two columns and three rows, generous cream margins, thin black panel borders, large condensed black serif title and small serif subtitle. Match the reference's exquisite painterly photoreal comic rendering, warm off-white Endless Museum galleries, polished floors, simple off-white plinths, shafts of sunlight, quiet pink accents, realistic hands, delicate shadows. Keep the same fictional adult student with short tousled dark hair, dusty burgundy knit top, black trousers and shoulder bag, and the same older grey-haired teacher in a dark blue jacket. They appear as avatars within the museum, no headset needed. The page must teach an operation through encounters, gesture and comparison. Use only the exact short captions specified, in large clean white caption boxes; code snippets are small museum teaching cards in readable monospaced lettering. Sparse speech, calm curiosity, material beauty. Preserve accurate diagram relationships. No test scores, no technical dashboards, no claim this is a photograph or actual runtime evidence. A book illustration, not a promotional poster.
Title exactly: "GIVE THE POINT A BODY". Subtitle: "Point One · A position, a surface, a boundary".
Panel 1 top-left: the student stands before an EMPTY museum plinth with an unobtrusive dashed cross at a position above it, an explanatory annotation not a physical object. Caption: "A position alone draws nothing." Small teaching card: "CENTRE = Vector3(0, 1.12, 0)".
Panel 2 top-right: a small beautiful white sphere now appears at that same position. The student's hand passes through this visible-only study, drawn with an intelligible translucent cutaway locally at the overlap. Caption: "A surface makes the point visible."
Panel 3 middle-left: a neighbouring solid white sphere, same appearance; the student approaching it is stopped at its collision boundary. An elegant dotted circle annotation shows the hidden physical boundary exactly matching the sphere, not a second physical object. Caption: "A boundary gives it contact."
Panel 4 middle-right: close-up of teacher holding a clear paper diagram. One top rectangle labelled "point" branches to two lower rectangles labelled "surface" and "boundary". Beside it the SAME small sphere shown in a refined cutaway overlay: visible skin and matching dotted collision circle, concentric, same radius. Caption: "Both belong to the point."
Panel 5 bottom-left: a controlled comparison on two plinths: white sphere radius 0.14 and white sphere radius 0.30, same centre height, the latter a little more than twice as wide. Dotted boundary overlays match each surface. Caption: "One radius changes both." Small card: "RADIUS: 0.14 → 0.30".
Panel 6 bottom-right: surface hidden again, student stopped by a faint dotted annotation of the boundary in empty air. Teacher looks on; preserve sunlight and shadows, no rendered white sphere here. Caption: "Invisible can still be solid."
Footer exactly: "What makes a point present: its address, its appearance, or what it stops?"

Title exactly: "TWO ENDS, ONE LINE". Subtitle: "Lines · Reuse the point; read the relation".

Caption: "One class. Two separate points." Small code card with two lines: "point = PointBody.new()" and "point_b = PointBody.new()".
Panel 2 top-right: student holds B and moves it diagonally above A; visible cylinder turns and changes length between the two centres. A small clear arrow goes from A to B. Card: "displacement = b - a". Caption: "From A to B."
Panel 3 middle-left: controlled vertical arrangement: B exactly one metre above A, points joined by an upright segment. A subtle comparison thumbnail shows the earlier one-metre horizontal span. Caption: "Same length. Another direction." Crisp readout: "DISTANCE 1.0".
Panel 4 middle-right: teacher and student compare three small arrangements in the gallery: two parallel pink bars, a plus, an X. Draw two finite bars for each; never create a node at the crossing just because they cross visually. Caption: "Arrange the relation." Small labels: "PARALLEL", "PLUS", "X".
Panel 5 bottom-left: show student stepping sideways around an apparent X. One bar lies in a plane slightly behind the other; an inset side view makes the depth separation explicit. The bars do NOT touch. Caption: "A crossing in view is not a shared point."
Panel 6 bottom-right: student has carried endpoint B around a detour then returned to its initial horizontal position; only the current straight pink span remains, no drawn history. Teacher's speech: "Where did the journey go?" Caption: "The line keeps only its current ends."

Title exactly: "KEEP THE JOURNEY". Subtitle: "Trace · Positions kept in order".
Panel 1 top-left: student carries the same small white pickable sphere along a short bent path. A thin pale-pink polygonal line remains behind it. Trace consists of straight segments, not a continuous magical fluid trail. Caption: "The same point. Now it leaves a record."
Panel 2 top-right: close teacher's paper, an ordered list with four clearly labelled slots "0", "1", "2", "3". Each slot stands for a stored position, with simple tiny vector marks. Student continues moving while the first entries stay fixed. Small code card: "positions.append(local_position)". Caption: "Keep the position, not the moving object."
Panel 3 middle-left: student holds the sphere still at end of short three-segment trace. Readout exactly "POINTS 4". No additional trace or new entries while motionless. Caption: "Holding still adds no new point."
Panel 4 middle-right: close comparison between last stored location, dotted circle, and current sphere moving at least five centimetres from it. A small measuring bracket labelled "5 cm". Card exactly "MIN_SEGMENT_DISTANCE = 0.05". Caption: "Keep another position after enough movement." This is a minimum distance, not forced equal spacing.
Panel 5 bottom-left: an elegant instructional close-up of four stored position marks, indexed 0,1,2,3, joined by EXACTLY three straight pink segments. A small paper diagram gives the three pairs: "0 → 1", "1 → 2", "2 → 3". Caption: "Four positions. Three neighbouring pairs." The stored markers are diagram annotations, not extra pickable bodies.
Panel 6 bottom-right: student and teacher compare the same bent movement drawn coarsely at threshold 0.20 and more finely at 0.05. Draw straight segments with irregular spacing; finer trace retains more corners, not every infinitesimal bend. Small labels "0.20" and "0.05". Caption: "What did the threshold leave out?"
Footer exactly: "The trace keeps positions in order. It does not keep every moment."

plates.title: GIVE THE RECORD ADDRESSES
concepts: Snapping in X, Y and Z
plates.summary: Keep the released pen drawing from the same museum session. Fit a copy to the display, then round its displayed positions onto a 3D lattice. The source world positions remain intact.
plates.alt: Six-panel museum comic: a released pen drawing is retained, a copied record is fitted to the display, a green version is snapped in three dimensions, and changing the interval changes the displayed result.

Title exactly: "GIVE THE RECORD ADDRESSES". Subtitle: "Grid · Keep the drawing; change its display".
Panel 1: student has just released the museum drawing pen, then sees the same bent pink drawing above a ruled field in the next hall. This is a PEN drawing transferred through the museum's supplied session store, not an invented file save for the pickable sphere. Teacher's speech: "Use this session's drawing." Caption: "Release in Trace. Continue in Grid." A nearby card reads "THIS SESSION".
Panel 2: teacher holds a paper labelled "SOURCE (WORLD)" with an ordered list of recorded positions represented by index slots and small vector marks, not made-up numeric values. A duplicate sheet goes toward a drawing display while the original stays. Caption: "Copy the record. Keep the source." Small code card: "new_trace = points.duplicate()".
Panel 3: diagram shows an off-centre small bent drawing fitted around the centre of a larger presentation field. Translation to the drawing's bounding-box centre happens BEFORE the scale change; two short arrows labelled "centre" and "scale". Caption: "Fit the drawing to the display." Code card: "(p - center) * final_scale".
Panel 4: student examines two related POLYLINES above the grid floor: pink for fitted retained positions, green for their rounded positions. They retain different Y heights; green does not flatten to the floor. Use subtle faint dotted vertical lattice guides to show X,Y,Z addresses. Both polylines consist of straight segments, not magical smooth curves. Caption: "Pink is fitted. Green is rounded." Small diagram card: "X · Y · Z".
Panel 5: teacher holds a controlled one-metre ruler comparison: first ruler subdivided into EXACTLY SIX equal intervals, seven ticks; second ruler into EXACTLY THREE equal intervals, four ticks. Labels "6 subdivisions" and "3 subdivisions". Alongside, the green trace becomes coarser while the pink fitted source remains the same. Caption: "Change the interval, not the source."
Panel 6: close look at a bend in the retained pink trace and its coarser green version; selected neighbours can round to the same lattice address. Student asks: "Which differences remain?" Caption: "Finer addresses cannot restore an unrecorded bend."
Footer exactly: "Index: which sample. Address: where on a lattice."

plates.title: THREE CORNERS, THEN A FACE
plates.summary: Select three positions from the original trace. Connect the corners, then add a triangular face. Compare changes of viewpoint with a true loss of area, and keep surface and collision distinct.
plates.alt: Six-panel museum comic: three selected trace positions form a closed triangle, a face is added, an edge-on view differs from three collinear corners, and handles have collision while the face does not.

plates.title: WHICH FACES MAKE AN INSIDE?
plates.summary: Retain three corners and add a fourth outside their plane. A face list chooses their connections. Add the missing row to close a tetrahedron, then move a shared vertex and follow its neighbouring faces.
plates.alt: Six-panel museum comic: four non-coplanar vertices support three open faces, face-index rows describe connections, one new row closes a tetrahedron, and moving a shared vertex changes its incident faces.

Title exactly: "WHICH FACES MAKE AN INSIDE?". Subtitle: "Polyhedra · Positions and connections".
A tetrahedron has FOUR vertices and FOUR triangular faces. An open trihedron uses the same four vertices but only THREE faces. Ensure these counts exactly; no five-vertex pyramids.
Panel 1: teacher and student beside four pink handles numbered 0,1,2,3. Positions 1,2,3 form a base triangle; position 0 is a new apex clearly outside their plane, making a skew tetrahedral arrangement. Caption: "Keep the three corners. Add one in depth."
Panel 2: three pale triangular faces meet at apex 0, each spanning one base edge, while the opening across 1,2,3 remains visibly empty toward the viewer. A clean paper diagram inset ensures the open topology is obvious. Caption: "Three faces meet at 0. One side stays open."
Panel 3: teacher shows the face list on a readable card with EXACT rows "[0, 1, 2]", "[0, 2, 3]", "[0, 3, 1]". Student follows one triangle with a finger outside its surface. The same vertex may be used by neighbouring faces. Caption: "Indices choose which positions meet."
Panel 4: same arrangement, unchanged corners, now a fourth face visibly spans the open base. Code card: "[1, 3, 2]". Caption: "One row closes the opening." The closed object is an irregular tetrahedron, not necessarily equal-edged.
Panel 5: student moves apex handle 0 sideways. All THREE incident side faces change, while the base triangle 1,2,3 remains fixed. Use one small dotted arrow from the previous apex to the new apex; no extra physical vertex. Caption: "Move one vertex. Its neighbouring faces change." Teacher asks: "Which rows use this index?"
Panel 6: elegant cutaway diagram of the closed tetrahedron showing an EMPTY interior and thin rendered faces, plus a dotted collider on one small handle only. The mathematical enclosure adds no filled material or face collider. Caption: "Enclosed by faces. Not filled with matter." Small card: "Only handles have colliders."
Footer exactly: "A hole can be an omitted connection."

plates.title: THE DIAGONAL WAS ALREADY THERE
plates.summary: Read a square face as two triangles. Move a shared corner to reveal its hidden diagonal, then change the connection list while retaining the same corner positions. A vertex edit differs from a transform of the whole object.
plates.alt: Six-panel museum comic: a cube's square face is divided into white and pink triangles, moving corner 6 reveals a crease along diagonal 5–7, and the alternate diagonal 4–6 changes the surface between the same corners.
